title: The Rules of an Enemy's Gate
story:
The five hills of Girivraja ringed the capital of Magadha like the fingers of a cupped hand: Vaihara, Varaha, Vrishava, Rishigiri, and Chaitya, the last of them best loved of all, worshipped by the citizens and by the royal line of Vrihadratha. Krishna had pointed them out as the three brothers drew near, and had shown Arjuna the city the way a man shows a treasure he means to take. Filled with flocks and herds, its water never failing, adorned with fine mansions standing in excellent array, free from every kind of calamity — a city, he said, that its king believed impregnable. "We shall, however, by slaying him today, humble his pride."

They did not enter by the gate. At the foot of the Chaityaka hill the brothers had set their hands to the rock and torn down the peak the whole city honoured, at the very point where the great drums of Vrihadratha used to sound, once beaten, for a full month. Then, in the guise of Brahmanas, with their bare arms as their only weapons, they had walked through the crowded streets, past shops heavy with edibles and wreaths, snatched garlands from the flower-vendors, and gone in decked like princes of the road. Their arms, smeared with sandal paste, looked like the trunks of sala trees. Passing through three gates that were crowded with men, they had come on proudly and cheerfully, like Himalayan lions eyeing cattle-folds, and the people of Magadha, seeing these giants in mendicants' robes, had wondered much.

Within the city, the learned Brahmanas had already seen evil omens and reported them. Jarasandha's priest had made the king mount an elephant and whirled lighted brands about him, and the king had begun a sacrifice with proper vows and fasts to turn the portents aside. Yet when the three strangers presented themselves at his abode, he rose up in haste and received them with every honour — water to wash their feet, honey, the offerings of the arghya, gifts of cattle — and bade them welcome. Bhima and Arjuna stood silent, and Krishna spoke for them. But the king was not a man to let a strange entry pass unremarked, and when the ceremony of welcome was done, he looked at his three guests and asked what they meant by coming into his city by no proper gate.

Krishna answered without heat, as though stating a rule of grammar. "These are the rules of the ordinance," he said. "An enemy's abode should be entered through a wrong gate, and a friend's abode through the right one." Then he added what no guest in that hall could have expected: "Know, O monarch, that this also is our eternal vow — that having entered the foe's abode for the accomplishment of our purpose, we accept not the worship offered to us."

The water for the feet stood untouched. The gifts lay where they had been laid. The king of Magadha, who had risen to greet these men as guests, had just been told, in the most courteous words imaginable, that they were his enemies: that they had entered his house the way one enters an enemy's house, and that they refused his friendship outright. Whatever courtesy had passed between them was over. What remained was the purpose for which they had come.

He heard it in silence. And in that silence, the three brothers stood in the hall of the king they had crossed a mountain to kill, their errand spoken aloud at last, with nothing left between them and it but the word of a king who had not yet given his answer.
reflection: Krishna answers a charge of bad manners with a precise code of his own: a friend's house and a foe's house are not entered the same way, and a guest who refuses the offered worship is declaring, openly and without rudeness, that he has come as an enemy. The courtliness of the reply only sharpens the threat beneath it.
next_story_tease: But Jarasandha, certain of his own innocence, would demand to know what injury he had ever done them.
hero_scene: Krishna standing calm in Jarasandha's hall, the untouched water for the feet and the gifts of welcome lying between him and the seated king, with Bhima and Arjuna silent behind him in mendicants' robes.
